Mustafa Sa'eed's story is Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness' reversed — the 'savage' goes to Europe and conquers it through seduction. The Arab Literary Academy named it the greatest Arabic novel of the 20th century.

exploreAction.targetName: Season of Migration to the North, chapters 1-5
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first five chapters. The narrator discovers Mustafa Sa'eed, a mysterious older man who quotes English poetry in a Sudanese village. Sa'eed's story emerges: a brilliant student sent to England who seduced English women as revenge for colonialism and was tried for murder of a woman he drove to suicide. Salih's prose is hypnotic — the Nile flows through every page. The novel asks: can the colonized ever go home?

name: A Visit from the Goon Squad (2010)
teaser: Jennifer Egan's novel told in 13 interlinked stories, including one chapter written entirely as a PowerPoint presentation. It spans from the 1970s punk scene to a near-future New York, following Bennie Salazar, a record executive, and Sasha, his kleptomaniac assistant. Won the Pulitzer. Time is the 'goon squad' — it takes everything eventually.

exploreAction.targetName: A Visit from the Goon Squad, chapters 1-4
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first four chapters. Sasha steals a wallet on a date. Bennie sprays gold flakes in his coffee and can't feel music anymore. Each chapter shifts perspective and time, but characters recur in the background. The PowerPoint chapter (Chapter 12) is not a gimmick — each slide is a short story. Egan writes the music industry as a metaphor for aging: everyone's trying to stay relevant as time closes in.

name: Pachinko (2017)
teaser: Min Jin Lee's multi-generational novel about a Korean family in Japan from 1910 to the 1980s. Koreans in Japan — Zainichi — were treated as permanent foreigners even after generations. The novel was rejected by every major publisher before becoming a National Book Award finalist. The title refers to pachinko parlors — one of the few businesses Zainichi Koreans could own.

exploreAction.targetName: Pachinko, Book I
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book I. Sunja, a teenager in a Korean fishing village, becomes pregnant by a married yakuza. A Christian minister offers to marry her and take her to Japan. Lee embeds the history of Japanese colonization of Korea in the smallest domestic moments: a bowl of rice, a boarding house, the registry that marks Koreans as aliens. The novel spans three generations; each one carries the weight of the previous.

name: The Canterbury Tales (c. 1400)
teaser: Geoffrey Chaucer's collection of 24 stories told by pilgrims traveling to Canterbury Cathedral. Each pilgrim tells a tale — knight, miller, wife of Bath, pardoner — in their own voice. Chaucer wrote in Middle English when that was revolutionary: French and Latin were the languages of literature. He died before finishing it; the tales we have are a fragment.

exploreAction.targetName: The Canterbury Tales, the General Prologue + 3 tales
exploreAction.instruction: Read the General Prologue and three tales: The Knight's Tale, The Miller's Tale, and The Wife of Bath's Tale. Each pilgrim is introduced in a portrait of startling vividness — the Prioress who feeds her dogs better than the poor, the Friar who's more pimp than priest. The Miller's Tale is a fabliau about a cuckolded carpenter — it's filthy and hilarious. Notice the Wife of Bath: she's been married five times and has the best argument for female sovereignty in medieval literature.

name: Austerlitz (2001)
teaser: W.G. Sebald's final novel about a man who arrives in England on a Kindertransport at age 4 and doesn't learn his real name or origin until he's retired. The novel is narrated as a series of conversations, accompanied by uncaptioned photographs — they feel like evidence but prove nothing. Sebald died in a car crash weeks after finishing it.

exploreAction.targetName: Austerlitz, the whole novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the whole novel — it's one long paragraph punctuated by photographs. Jacques Austerlitz, an architectural historian, tells his story to the narrator in train stations and cafes across Europe. He was a child refugee from Prague; his mother died in Theresienstadt. Sebald's sentences are immense — they hold decades in one breath. The photographs are uncaptioned: a building, a boy in a costume, a pair of eyes. They haunt the text without explaining it.

name: A Wizard of Earthsea (1968)
teaser: Ursula K. Le Guin's fantasy novel about a boy named Ged who goes to a wizard school and releases a shadow monster in an act of pride. He spends the rest of the novel being hunted by his own darkness. Le Guin wrote it as a response to the lack of non-white heroes in fantasy — all the characters in Earthsea are brown-skinned. It was published decades before Harry Potter and says more about the danger of magical power in 200 pages than Rowling does in 7 books.

exploreAction.targetName: A Wizard of Earthsea, the whole novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the whole novel. Ged, a goatherd with a gift for magic, is trained at the school of Roke. In a duel of pride, he summons a shadow from the land of the dead. The shadow pursues him; eventually he realizes he must stop running and turn to face it. The novel is structured like a Taoist parable: the shadow is Ged's own death, and naming it is the only way to be free. Le Guin's magic has moral weight — every spell has consequences.

name: The Bluest Eye (1970)
teaser: Toni Morrison's debut novel about Pecola Breedlove, a Black girl who prays for blue eyes, believing they will make her beautiful and loved. The novel is told in fragments — from multiple perspectives, across years — because Pecola's trauma can't be narrated in a straight line. Morrison wrote it while working as an editor at Random House, getting up at 4 AM to write before her children woke.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bluest Eye, the whole novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the whole novel. The novel opens with a Dick-and-Jane primer that fractures into nonsense — the safe white world is breaking apart. Pecola's story is told by Claudia, a girl who survives what Pecola doesn't. Morrison shows racism as a poison that turns inward: Pecola believes if she had blue eyes, she would be beautiful. The novel's tragedy is not just what happens to Pecola but that her community participates in destroying her.

name: Braiding Sweetgrass (2013)
teaser: Robin Wall Kimmerer's book about indigenous wisdom and botany. Kimmerer is a Potawatomi botanist and professor who bridges western science and Native knowledge. Each chapter weaves together ecology, storytelling, and memoir. The title comes from the Potawatomi story of Skywoman, who brought plants to earth. The book was a slow-burn bestseller that became a phenomenon years after publication.

exploreAction.targetName: Braiding Sweetgrass, Part One: Planting Sweetgrass
exploreAction.instruction: Read Part One. Kimmerer begins with Skywoman falling from the sky, creating Turtle Island with a handful of mud. Then she describes pecans, strawberries, and the grammar of animacy in Potawatomi — English treats the natural world as 'it'; Potawatomi treats it as someone. Notice how Kimmerer refuses to choose between science and spirituality: they are two languages for the same love. 'In some Native languages the term for plants translates to those who take care of us.'

name: On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous (2019)
teaser: Ocean Vuong's debut novel written as a letter from a Vietnamese-American son to his illiterate mother. Vuong is a poet, and the novel reads like a long poem — every sentence is chiseled. It moves between the Vietnam War, a nail salon in Hartford, and a first love with a white boy in tobacco fields. The novel is autobiographical in spirit but Vuong insists it's fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous, Part One
exploreAction.instruction: Read Part One. 'Let me begin again.' Little Dog writes to his mother Rose, who cannot read. He describes his grandmother Lan, who escaped an arranged marriage during the war, and his first love, Trevor, who taught him to drive a combine harvester. Vuong writes about the body — his mother's hands scarred from the nail salon, Trevor's body in the tobacco fields — as the site where love and violence are the same thing. The monarch butterfly is the novel's recurring image: migration, transformation, fragile beauty.

name: If Beale Street Could Talk (1974)
teaser: James Baldwin's novel about a young Black couple in 1970s Harlem — Tish and Fonny. Fonny is in prison for a rape he didn't commit, and Tish is pregnant with his child. The novel is narrated by Tish, whose voice is steady and fierce. Baldwin wrote it as a love story, not a protest novel — but love under racism is protest. Adapted into an Oscar-winning film in 2018.

exploreAction.targetName: If Beale Street Could Talk, the whole novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the whole novel. Tish tells Fonny — and us — how they fell in love. She's 19 and pregnant; her family rallies around Fonny while his own family fractures. Baldwin writes love as the only resistance that matters: Tish's family pools their money for lawyers, brings food, holds each other. The novel is about the carceral system but never lets the system overshadow the people. Tish's narration is the novel's miracle — she's never bitter, only certain.

name: The Vaster Wilds (2023)
teaser: Lauren Groff's novel about a servant girl who escapes a 17th-century colonial settlement in Virginia during a famine and runs into the wilderness with nothing but her wits. The novel is a survival story and a spiritual crisis told in prose that feels like scripture. Groff wrote it in a fever during the pandemic.

exploreAction.targetName: The Vaster Wilds, Part One
exploreAction.instruction: Read Part One. A girl known only as 'the girl' or 'the servant' flees the Jamestown settlement in the dead of winter. She has no name because she was never given one that mattered. The wilderness is violent — wolves, starvation, exposure — but also holy. Groff's prose is stripped to its essentials: every sentence is physical. The girl's spiritual crisis intensifies as she starves: she sees God in a flash of light on ice and questions whether God has ever seen her.

name: The Alchemist (1988)
teaser: Paulo Coelho's allegorical novel about Santiago, a Spanish shepherd who dreams of treasure at the pyramids. The novel was a slow seller at first — Coelho's first publisher dropped him — but has now sold over 65 million copies in 80+ languages. It's one of the best-selling books in history and the most translated book by a living author.

exploreAction.targetName: The Alchemist, Part One
exploreAction.instruction: Read Part One. Santiago sells his sheep and sails to Tangier. He's robbed, works for a crystal merchant, and joins a caravan crossing the Sahara. Coelho writes in simple declarative sentences — the prose feels like folklore. 'When you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.' The novel is less a plot than a parable: the treasure was never at the pyramids. Notice the alchemist himself appears only in the last third.

name: The Bee Sting (2023)
teaser: Paul Murray's novel about the Barnes family — an Irish family unraveling after the 2008 financial crash. The novel is structured in four parts, each from a different family member's perspective. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize. The novel is funny, devastating, and 650 pages that feel like 300.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bee Sting, Part One: Cass
exploreAction.instruction: Read Part One. Cass Barnes, 17, is drinking in the woods with her friend Elaine when the novel opens. Her father's car dealership is failing; her mother is selling things on eBay; her brother is building a bunker. Murray writes Irish family life with comic precision and then turns the screw: the financial crash is a slow-motion car wreck that everyone sees coming and no one can stop. The bee sting of the title is both literal and metaphorical.

name: The Midnight Library (2020)
teaser: Matt Haig's novel about Nora Seed, who tries to kill herself and finds herself in a library between life and death — each book contains a different version of her life she could have lived. The novel is about regret and the paths not taken. Haig wrote it after his own mental health crisis and it became a global bestseller.

exploreAction.targetName: The Midnight Library, the whole novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the whole novel. Nora lands in the Midnight Library presided over by her old school librarian Mrs. Elm. She can try any life — Olympic swimmer, rock star, glaciologist, mother — and if she finds one worth living, she stays. The premise is simple but Haig executes it with empathy: each life teaches Nora something about the one she already has. The novel's philosophy is not 'anything is possible' but 'what you have is already enough.'

name: Kindred (1979)
teaser: Octavia Butler's novel about Dana, a Black woman in 1976 Los Angeles who is suddenly transported to a Maryland plantation in 1815. She is pulled back in time whenever her white ancestor Rufus is in mortal danger — she must keep him alive long enough to father her ancestor. Butler called it 'grim fantasy' — there's no explanation for the time travel, just the unflinching reality of slavery.

exploreAction.targetName: Kindred, the whole novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the whole novel. Dana's first trip to the past: she saves a drowning white boy named Rufus and is nearly shot by his father. The time travel is involuntary and brutal — Dana arrives disoriented and returns with injuries. Butler doesn't romanticize the past: Dana must live as a slave, and the novel documents the daily violence without flinching. Rufus grows from a frightened boy into a slaveholder who believes he owns Dana. The horror is not the time travel; it's history.

name: Yellowface (2023)
teaser: R.F. Kuang's novel about June Hayward, a white writer who steals her dead Chinese-American friend's manuscript and publishes it as her own — complete with an ethnically ambiguous author photo. What follows is a satire of the publishing industry, cancel culture, and literary appropriation. The novel went viral on BookTok and became a bestseller.

exploreAction.targetName: Yellowface, the whole novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the whole novel. Athena Liu dies choking on a pancake in front of June, who takes her unpublished manuscript about Chinese laborers in WWI. June edits it, changes her name to Juniper Song, and becomes a literary star. The novel works as thriller and satire: June's narration is a masterclass in self-justification. Kuang makes you understand June even as you recoil. The publishing industry — sensitivity readers, Twitter pile-ons, diversity panels — is skewered with insider knowledge.

name: The Sellout (2015)
teaser: Paul Beatty's novel about a Black man who reinstates slavery and segregation in his Los Angeles neighborhood — as satire — and ends up in the Supreme Court. Won the Booker Prize (the first American to win it). Every sentence is a joke that's serious. Beatty's narrator is an urban farmer who grows satsumas and watermelons and calls himself a 'sellout' for loving the neighborhood no one else cares about.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sellout, chapters 1-8
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first eight chapters. The narrator (unnamed) is raised by a sociologist father who used him as a subject in racial psychology experiments. His father is shot by the police, and the narrator's response is absurdity: he takes a slave, paints a line of segregation on the street. Beatty's prose is hip-hop and literature at once — dense with references, profane, hilarious. The satire is so sharp it hurts: the novel is about how race is simultaneously everything and nothing.

name: Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937)
teaser: Zora Neale Hurston's novel about Janie Crawford's journey through three marriages to selfhood in rural Florida. Out of print for decades, rescued in 1975 by Alice Walker, who put a gravestone on Hurston's unmarked grave. The novel is written in lyrical third person and Black Southern dialect — the two registers are the novel's music.

exploreAction.targetName: Their Eyes Were Watching God, chapters 1-6
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first six chapters. Janie returns to Eatonville and tells her story. Her grandmother marries her off at 16 — she 'had been summoned to behold a revelation.' Janie's journey is toward the horizon: not a man but a self. Hurston's prose is incantatory: 'Ships at a distance have every man's wish on board.' The hurricane section is one of the most terrifying passages in American literature. Janie survives it all — and the novel ends with her pulling in her horizon 'like a great fish-net.'

name: Les Misérables
teaser: Victor Hugo's 1862 epic of a former convict, a bishop's mercy, and a police inspector's obsession — the great novel of grace versus law, set against the barricades of 1832 Paris.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the bishop and the candlesticks
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where the Bishop of Digne shelters Jean Valjean and forgives the theft. Notice how Hugo prepares the moral engine of the whole book in these pages. Write what the candlesticks come to mean each time they reappear.

name: The Count of Monte Cristo
teaser: Alexandre Dumas's 1844 masterpiece of wrongful imprisonment and long, patient revenge — Edmond Dantès escapes the Château d'If and returns as the mysterious Count to dismantle his betrayers.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the betrayal and the prison
exploreAction.instruction: Read Dantès's arrest and his meeting with the Abbé Faria in prison. Notice how Dumas turns a false accusation into an education. Write how the years of imprisonment make the revenge that follows both sweeter and more terrible.

name: Candide
teaser: Voltaire's 1759 razor of a novella — a young optimist dragged through war, shipwreck, Inquisition, and Eldorado, learning that this is not the best of all possible worlds. The cure for Pangloss is still in print.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters, then the conclusion
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters where Pangloss teaches 'all for the best,' then jump to the famous ending. Notice how the horrors arrive in deadpan, fast sequence. Write what 'we must cultivate our garden' really proposes.

name: The Scarlet Letter
teaser: Nathaniel Hawthorne's 1850 novel of Puritan Boston — Hester Prynne stands on the scaffold with her infant and her embroidered 'A,' while her secret co-sinner watches from the crowd. America's first great psychological novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the prison door and the marketplace
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters, including the rosebush by the prison door. Notice how Hawthorne turns symbols — the letter, the rose, the scaffold — into characters. Write what the 'A' means to Hester, to the town, and finally to the reader.

name: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
teaser: Mark Twain's 1884 masterpiece — a boy and an escaped man float the Mississippi on a raft, and Huck must decide whether his conscience or his society is right. Hemingway called it the source of all American literature.

exploreAction.targetName: The raft chapters and the 'All right, then, I'll go to hell' moment
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Huck tears up the letter to Miss Watson. Notice how Twain lets Huck's decision stay half-wrong even as it is right. Write about the moment the raft becomes a place of moral freedom.

name: Little Women
teaser: Louisa May Alcott's 1868 novel of the four March sisters in Civil War New England — Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy growing up through poverty, illness, ambition, and love. It made Jo March the model of the writer-girl.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Christmas and the mother's letter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters, where the sisters sacrifice their breakfasts for a poor family. Notice how Alcott balances idealism with sharp sibling realism. Write what each sister's temperament contributes to the household's economy.

name: Middlemarch
teaser: George Eliot's 1872 novel of provincial life — Dorothea Brooke's high ideals, Tertius Lydgate's research, and the whole town of Middlemarch gossiping, marrying, and reforming. Virginia Woolf called it one of the few English novels for grown-ups.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Dorothea and Casaubon
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Dorothea marries the elderly Casaubon out of idealistic hunger. Notice how Eliot narrates self-deception with immense sympathy. Write how the novel's title — a provincial town — becomes a portrait of the human lot.

name: Bleak House
teaser: Charles Dickens's 1853 attack on the Court of Chancery — the endless lawsuit Jarndyce and Jarndyce eats generations alive while fog and dust settle over London. A detective story, a love story, and a legal horror show.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the fog and the court
exploreAction.instruction: Read the famous opening, where fog wraps the High Court of Chancery. Notice how Dickens doubles his narration between Esther's voice and an omniscient present tense. Write how the lawsuit functions as the novel's true villain.

name: Vanity Fair
teaser: Thackeray's 1848 'novel without a hero' — Becky Sharp claws her way up society with wit and no conscience while Amelia Sedley waits, loyal and dim. The great comic novel of social climbing.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Becky leaves school with her skills
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Becky throws the dictionary out of the coach window. Notice how Thackeray's narrator keeps winking at the reader from the puppet booth. Write how the novel makes us root for a thoroughly unprincipled heroine.

name: Dracula
teaser: Bram Stoker's 1897 epistolary horror novel assembled the vampire legend — diary entries, telegrams, and phonograph records tracking the Count from Transylvania to London, and the band that hunts him back to his castle.

exploreAction.targetName: Jonathan Harker's first journal entries in Transylvania
exploreAction.instruction: Read Harker's journal, where hospitality curdles into imprisonment. Notice how Stoker withholds the Count's reveal and then springs it. Write how the frame of documents makes the horror feel reported rather than invented.

name: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
teaser: Robert Louis Stevenson's 1886 novella of the door, the will, and the doctor who drinks to become his own worst self. A hundred pages that gave the English language its name for the double life.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella — especially the last chapter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the story through, saving Jekyll's 'Full Statement of the Case' for last. Notice how every earlier chapter is a clue to the confession. Write what the novella suggests about respectability and the selves we keep locked.

name: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
teaser: Lewis Carroll's 1865 dream-novel of a girl who falls down a rabbit hole into a world of logic turned upside down — the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter, the Queen of Hearts. Nonsense with a system.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — down the rabbit hole and the pool of tears
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters. Notice how Carroll plays with size, words, and the rules of games. Write how the book's logic-inversion works — what does it mean that Wonderland is unreasonable by the very rules of reason?

name: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
teaser: L. Frank Baum's 1900 American fairy tale — Dorothy, Toto, and the cyclone into a land of Munchkins, scarecrows, and emerald cities. Far stranger and more political than the movie everyone remembers.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the cyclone and the yellow brick road
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters. Notice how Baum keeps the wonder precise — each country has a color and a problem. Write how the book's structure (a quest with companions who each lack something) became the template for a century of stories.

name: Anne of Green Gables
teaser: L. M. Montgomery's 1908 novel of the red-haired orphan who talks too much and dreams too big on Prince Edward Island. Marilla and Matthew wanted a boy; they got Anne Shirley, and so did the world.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the orphan's arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read Anne's first conversation with Marilla, where she renames the avenue 'the White Way of Delight.' Notice how Montgomery uses speech to build character. Write what Anne's imagination does for the practical Cuthberts.

name: The Secret Garden
teaser: Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1911 novel — sour Mary Lennox, orphaned in India, comes to Yorkshire and finds a locked garden and a sickly cousin. The garden heals them all, one buried bulb at a time.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Mary arrives in Yorkshire
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters. Notice how the Yorkshire dialect and the moor feel like a new climate for a spoiled child. Write how the secret garden works as both place and metaphor — what is growing back in each character?

name: Peter and Wendy
teaser: J. M. Barrie's 1911 novel of the boy who never grows up — the Darling nursery, the second star to the right, and the pirate captain who fears the crocodile and the clock it swallowed.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the nursery and the flight to Neverland
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters. Notice how Barrie's narrator keeps addressing the reader directly and gently. Write what the book really thinks about growing up — is Peter's refusal freedom or tragedy?

name: Treasure Island
teaser: Robert Louis Stevenson's 1883 adventure novel that set the template for pirate fiction — Jim Hawkins, Long John Silver, and the map of an island where X marks the spot. One-legged villains have never recovered.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Admiral Benbow and the black spot
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters. Notice how Stevenson builds menace from the old seaman's arrival. Write how Jim's boy's-eye view makes the story at once innocent and chilling, and what makes Silver such a magnetic villain.

name: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas
teaser: Jules Verne's 1870 underwater voyage — Professor Aronnax, harpooner Ned Land, and the mysterious Captain Nemo aboard the Nautilus, touring the world's oceans as science, wonder, and vengeance.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the monster hunt
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters. Notice how Verne feeds the reader catalogs of marine life while advancing the mystery of Nemo. Write how the Nautilus represents both liberation and prison — what does Nemo want from the sea?

name: Notes from Underground
teaser: Dostoevsky's 1864 novella that opened modern literature — a spiteful, brilliant narrator argues from his basement against reason, progress, and the Crystal Palace. The anti-hero's birth certificate.

exploreAction.targetName: Part One — the Underground Man's manifesto
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first part, where the narrator announces that two times two makes five. Notice how he performs his own self-contempt. Write what the Underground Man's hatred of the 'sublime and beautiful' reveals about freedom and spite.

name: The Idiot
teaser: Dostoevsky's 1869 novel of a 'positively beautiful man' — Prince Myshkin returns to Petersburg and his goodness detonates the society around him, especially in his love for the tormented Nastasya Filippovna.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Myshkin's return and the party scene
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, from the train to the general's house. Notice how Myshkin's candor disarms everyone and threatens everything. Write why the novel's author called his hero an attempt to depict a truly good man.

name: Faust
teaser: Goethe's lifelong masterpiece, published in parts from 1808 to 1832 — a scholar bets his soul against a moment of true contentment, and the devil's wager tests the meaning of striving itself.

exploreAction.targetName: The Prologue in Heaven and Faust's opening monologue
exploreAction.instruction: Read the wager scene and Faust's despair at book learning. Notice how Goethe reworks the medieval legend into a modern question. Write what the Prologue in Heaven's bet between God and Mephistopheles suggests about human striving.

name: The Stranger
teaser: Albert Camus's 1942 novel of Meursault, who kills a man on a sunlit beach and is judged less for the crime than for not crying at his mother's funeral. The defining novel of the absurd.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the funeral and the beach
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Meursault describes his mother's death with flat precision. Notice how the style embodies the worldview. Write how the trial in Part Two convicts Meursault of failing to perform grief — what does that reveal?

name: Doctor Zhivago
teaser: Pasternak's 1957 novel of the doctor-poet Yuri Zhivago across revolution and war — and his love for Lara, a love that survives history and is destroyed by it. The novel that cost its author the Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the funeral and the first meeting
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Yuri's childhood and his first glimpse of Lara are established. Notice how Pasternak's prose is lyrical even in sorrow. Write how the novel treats the individual against the tide of history — and why it was banned.

name: And Quiet Flows the Don
teaser: Sholokhov's 1928 epic of the Cossack Grigory Melekhov through the First World War, the revolution, and the civil war — a river of a novel about a people and a man torn between loyalties.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Melekhov household
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the village and the family are established against the Don's flow. Notice how Sholokhov grounds the epic in one farmstead. Write what the river means to the novel — continuity, change, or the indifference of nature.

name: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
teaser: Solzhenitsyn's 1962 novella of a single day in a Soviet labor camp — breakfast, work, soup, and survival, from dawn to lights-out. The book that made the gulag visible to the world.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, from the morning bell to the last spoon of soup. Notice how Solzhenitsyn finds dignity in the smallest routines of the camp. Write what the novel achieves by limiting itself to one ordinary day of suffering.

name: Cancer Ward
teaser: Solzhenitsyn's 1968 novel set in a Soviet cancer ward — where the disease becomes the honest metaphor for the system, and patients debate politics, truth, and survival between treatments.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the arrival at the ward
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Oleg Kostoglotov enters the ward and meets its inmates. Notice how Solzhenitsyn uses the illness to strip away pretense. Write how the ward becomes a compressed model of the larger society.

name: We
teaser: Zamyatin's 1924 dystopia of the One State — D-503's numbered happiness and his forbidden soul, in the glass city that taught Orwell and Huxley their blueprints. The grandfather of all dystopias.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening records
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening records, where the narrator's numbered life is described with mechanical pride. Notice how the diary form enacts the state's control of language. Write how the novel's ideas — happiness versus freedom — were stolen and refined by its successors.

name: The Heart of the Matter
teaser: Graham Greene's 1948 novel of Scobie, an honest colonial policeman in wartime West Africa, trapped between pity, adultery, and his Catholic faith — the 'entertainment' that became Greene's most controversial masterpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the colony and the pity
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Scobie's burden of pity is established. Notice how Greene narrates sin and mercy with terrible intimacy. Write what the novel says about pity as a motive — and whether Scobie's end is damnation or mercy.

name: The Power and the Glory
teaser: Greene's 1940 novel of the last priest in a Mexican state where the Church is outlawed — a whiskey priest, a coward and a saint, hunted across the heat. Greene called it his favorite of his own books.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the priest on the run
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the whiskey priest's flight begins in a provincial town. Notice how Greene makes the priest's sinfulness inseparable from his vocation. Write what the novel suggests about holiness appearing in the most unworthy vessel.

name: Brideshead Revisited
teaser: Evelyn Waugh's 1945 novel of memory, faith, and the Marchmain family — Charles Ryder's love for Sebastian and the golden world of Brideshead, recollected during the war. Waugh's most tender book.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the army and the memory
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the wartime narrator rediscovers Brideshead. Notice how Waugh frames the story as memory within memory. Write what the novel says about grace, and about loving people who cannot be saved by love alone.

name: Decline and Fall
teaser: Waugh's 1928 debut — Paul Pennyfeather is expelled from Oxford for running in his trousers and falls upward into a world of schoolmasters, society hostesses, and Welsh builders. The novel that made Waugh a name.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the expulsion and the school
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the toppling of Paul's life is narrated with perfect deadpan. Notice how Waugh's comedy is built from the gap between what happens and how it is reported. Write what the novel's title says about the world Paul keeps surviving.

name: A Handful of Dust
teaser: Waugh's 1934 novel of Tony Last, whose wife's affair sends him into the jungle of British Guiana — where he reads Dickens aloud forever to a madman. The cruelest ending in English comic fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Hetton and the affair
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Tony's gothic manor and his wife's boredom are established. Notice how Waugh moves from drawing-room comedy to nightmare. Write how the ending's absurd horror completes the novel's view of love and duty.

name: Lucky Jim
teaser: Kingsley Amis's 1954 comic novel of Jim Dixon, a junior lecturer tormented by his professor — the funniest book of the angry-young-man era, built around one unforgettable hungover lecture.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the hangover and the professor
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jim's misery and his invented 'Dixon face' are established. Notice how Amis turns academic servitude into slapstick. Write what the novel's comedy says about class, and why the lecture scene remains a classic of farce.

name: The Woman in White
teaser: Wilkie Collins's 1860 sensation novel — a woman in white on a moonlit road, an identity swap, and a conspiracy told through a chorus of documents. The book that made Victorian readers stay up all night.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the meeting on the road
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the artist Walter Hartright meets the woman in white. Notice how Collins builds suspense through multiple narrators and withheld facts. Write how the novel's epistolary structure keeps the mystery alive chapter after chapter.

name: The Moonstone
teaser: Collins's 1868 novel, often called the first English detective novel — a stolen diamond, a cursed night, and Sergeant Cuff's slow, patient detection across a Yorkshire house party. Detection as a form of love.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the diamond and the birthday
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Moonstone's curse and its theft are established. Notice how Collins uses multiple narrators to keep the reader guessing. Write what the novel's invention — the detective who notices small things — gave to the genre.

name: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
teaser: Conan Doyle's 1892 first collection of Holmes stories — A Scandal in Bohemia, The Red-Headed League, and ten more cases that made the detective and his methods part of the world's imagination.

exploreAction.targetName: A Scandal in Bohemia and The Red-Headed League
exploreAction.instruction: Read two of the stories. Notice how Holmes's deductions are demonstrated rather than merely claimed — and how the collection's 'the woman' introduces Irene Adler. Write what makes Holmes's method — observation plus deduction — so satisfying as narrative.

name: The Hound of the Baskervilles
teaser: Conan Doyle's 1902 novel of the Dartmoor curse — a spectral hound, a dead heir, and Holmes away while Watson investigates the moor. The perfect Gothic detective story, and the most loved Sherlock Holmes novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the manuscript and the moor
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the legend of the hound and the arrival of Sir Henry are established. Notice how Doyle makes the moor itself a character. Write how the novel balances the supernatural explanation and the rational one.

name: And Then There Were None
teaser: Agatha Christie's 1939 novel of ten strangers on an island who die one by one to a nursery rhyme — the best-selling mystery of all time, and the purest whodunit ever constructed.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the island and the accusation
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the guests arrive at Soldier Island and the gramophone accuses them all. Notice how Christie eliminates suspects while multiplying suspicion. Write what the nursery rhyme structure contributes to the novel's dread.

name: Murder on the Orient Express
teaser: Christie's 1934 novel of a murder in a snowbound train car and twelve suspects — the case that forces Poirot to choose between the law and justice. The most ingenious of her locked-room puzzles.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the train and the murder
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Orient Express is stranded and Ratchett is found dead. Notice how Christie manages twelve suspects without losing the reader. Write what the famous solution says about the relationship between justice and law.

name: Rebecca
teaser: Daphne du Maurier's 1938 novel of the nameless second Mrs. de Winter, the house Manderley, and the dead first wife who still rules it — a Gothic romance about the ghosts of marriage.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the meeting and Manderley
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the narrator marries Maxim and arrives at Manderley. Notice how du Maurier makes the house and Rebecca's absence into characters. Write what 'Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again' promises about memory and haunting.

name: Jamaica Inn
teaser: du Maurier's 1936 novel of Mary Yellan, sent to her aunt's Cornish inn on the moors — where the landlord runs a wrecking crew and the storms hide worse. A Gothic thriller of wind, dread, and survival.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journey to the inn
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Mary's ride across the moor and her arrival at the inn set the tone. Notice how du Maurier makes the landscape hostile and alive. Write how the inn's isolation and its secrets feed each other.

name: To the Lighthouse
teaser: Woolf's 1927 novel of the Ramsay family's summers on the Isle of Skye — the trip to the lighthouse postponed, the mother's death, and time passing like weather. The modernist novel at its most luminous.

exploreAction.targetName: The Window section and Time Passes
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening section, where Mrs. Ramsay's dinner holds the family together, then Time Passes. Notice how Woolf renders what is not said. Write what the lighthouse means to each character — and what arriving there at the end completes.

name: Orlando
teaser: Woolf's 1928 fantasy-biography of a poet who lives for centuries and changes sex — a love letter to Vita Sackville-West, and the most playful of Woolf's novels. Time, gender, and glory as a game.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the boy and the centuries
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orlando moves from the Elizabethan court into the centuries. Notice how Woolf treats history as costume and gender as costume. Write what the novel's freedom from biography's rules allows it to say about identity.

name: A Room of One's Own
teaser: Woolf's 1929 essay on women and fiction — the locked library, the imaginary Shakespeare's sister, and the famous claim that a woman needs money and a room of her own to write. The founding text of feminist criticism.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Beadle and the library
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the essay's narrator is turned away from the library and from the grass. Notice how Woolf turns argument into narrative. Write what 'Shakespeare's sister' illustrates about talent and circumstance.

name: A Passage to India
teaser: Forster's 1924 novel of Dr. Aziz, Mrs. Moore, and the Marabar Caves — a friendship across empire tested by accusation and echo. The novel that asked whether connection can survive politics.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mosque and the caves
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Aziz meets Mrs. Moore in the mosque, then read the cave scene. Notice how Forster withholds what happened in the cave. Write what the echo — 'boum' — represents, and why the novel refuses to resolve it.

name: Howards End
teaser: Forster's 1910 novel of the Schlegels, the Wilcoxes, and the house that means England — 'Only connect.' The novel of class, culture, and who inherits the land.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the house and the families
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the connection between the cultured Schlegels and the practical Wilcoxes is established. Notice how Forster turns the house into the novel's conscience. Write what 'only connect' asks of people divided by class.

name: Sons and Lovers
teaser: D. H. Lawrence's 1913 novel of Paul Morel, his coal-miner father, and the mother who claims his soul — the Oedipal novel that scandalized and defined modern English fiction. Class, passion, and the family knot.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mother and the sons
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the marriage of Walter and Gertrude Morel founders and the children become her consolation. Notice how Lawrence renders family feeling with raw intimacy. Write what the novel says about mothers, sons, and the women who come between.

name: Women in Love
teaser: Lawrence's 1920 sequel to Sons and Lovers — two sisters, two men, and the search for a love that is not possession, ending in the Alps. His most philosophical novel, and his most radical.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wedding and the sisters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Ursula and Gudrun meet Birkin and Gerald. Notice how Lawrence uses the wedding as a stage for his ideas about love and power. Write what the novel proposes love might be, beyond ownership.

name: Lady Chatterley's Lover
teaser: Lawrence's 1928 novel of Constance Chatterley and the gamekeeper Mellors — the most famous banned book of the 20th century, prosecuted for obscenity in 1960, and finally read as the tender novel it is.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the marriage and the estate
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Connie's sterile marriage to the paralyzed Clifford is established. Notice how Lawrence links the body's freedom to the book's politics. Write what the novel's frankness was really arguing against in 1928.

name: The Good Soldier
teaser: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel of two couples and nine years of friendship — 'the saddest story' told by the most unreliable narrator in fiction. Dowell's calm confession hides everything it reveals.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the confession begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Dowell announces the tragedy and then circles it. Notice how the narrator's omissions are the plot. Write what the novel's technique — telling everything and understanding nothing — says about marriage and memory.

name: Of Human Bondage
teaser: Maugham's 1915 semi-autobiographical novel of Philip Carey, the clubfoot and the artist's life — love for the impossible Mildred, poverty in Paris, and the slow education of the heart. The bildungsroman to end bildungsromans.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the school and the clubfoot
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Philip's disability and his orphanhood are established. Notice how Maugham narrates suffering with cool clarity. Write what Philip learns through his bondage to Mildred — and what the novel's ending forgives.

name: The Razor's Edge
teaser: Maugham's 1944 novel of Larry Darrell, who returns from the Great War and refuses the American dream to seek enlightenment in India — told by a narrator who is Maugham himself. The spiritual quest novel of its era.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the return and the refusal
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Larry's refusal of a career is met with bafflement. Notice how Maugham frames the quest through the society that cannot understand it. Write what the title's 'razor's edge' — the hard path — means in the novel.

name: Brighton Rock
teaser: Greene's 1938 novel of Pinkie, a teenage gangster in Brighton who believes in hell — and of the girl who knows too much. A thriller that is really a novel about damnation and mercy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the pier and the killing
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the murder and Pinkie's world are established. Notice how Greene uses the seaside's gaudy surface against the moral darkness. Write what Pinkie's Catholicism — his certainty of damnation — does to his choices.

name: The Quiet American
teaser: Greene's 1955 novel of Saigon in the early Vietnam years — Fowler the jaded journalist, Pyle the idealistic American, and the woman they both love. The novel that warned about American innocence abroad.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the body in the river
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Pyle's death is revealed and then narrated backward. Notice how Greene uses the love triangle to frame the politics. Write what the novel suggests about good intentions — and why it was hated when published.

name: Burmese Days
teaser: Orwell's 1934 first novel of the British Raj in Burma — the timber business, the club, and the one decent man trapped among racists. The novel that taught Orwell what empire was made of.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the club and the district
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the colonial club's petty hierarchies are established. Notice how Orwell exposes the racism that polite fiction of the time ignored. Write how the novel's firsthand anger shaped everything Orwell wrote later.

name: Down and Out in Paris and London
teaser: Orwell's 1933 memoir of poverty — the Paris kitchens, the London doss-houses, and the tramps' code of the road. The book that taught Orwell how the poor actually live, from the inside.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Paris hotel kitchen
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orwell works as a plongeur in a Paris hotel. Notice how he reports humiliation with dry precision. Write what the book's sociology of poverty — the tramp, the spike, the casual ward — gave to his later politics.

name: Homage to Catalonia
teaser: Orwell's 1938 account of fighting in the Spanish Civil War — the trenches, the lice, and the betrayal of the revolution by its own allies. The book that made him a socialist and a skeptic of all causes.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the militia and the front
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orwell joins the POUM militia and experiences the war's strange quiet. Notice how he narrates both the idealism and the absurdity. Write what the May Days in Barcelona taught him about power and truth.

name: The Brave Little Tailor and Other Tales
teaser: The Grimms' fairy tales of the tailor who kills seven flies and conquers giants — along with Rapunzel, Rumpelstiltskin, and the stories that shaped childhood for two centuries. The collected dark magic of the European folk tale.

exploreAction.targetName: A selection of tales, including The Brave Little Tailor
exploreAction.instruction: Read several tales, noticing how the Brothers Grimm preserved the stories' violence and wonder. Write what the tales assume about justice, luck, and the world — and why children have always needed their darkness.

name: The Little Prince
teaser: Saint-Exupéry's 1943 novella of a pilot stranded in the desert who meets a prince from a small planet — a fable about grown-ups, roses, and what is essential. The most translated book in the world after the Bible.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the drawing and the meeting
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the narrator's childhood drawing frames the whole book. Notice how the prince's questions expose the absurdity of adult priorities. Write what the book means by 'what is essential is invisible to the eye.'

name: Night
teaser: Elie Wiesel's 1958 memoir of his boyhood in Auschwitz and Buchenwald — the night his faith died with his father, and the silence that followed. The essential testimony of the Holocaust, in a voice that refuses comfort.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Sighet and the arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the community's denial gives way to the cattle cars and the selection. Notice how Wiesel's spare prose carries the enormity without melodrama. Write what the memoir says about the silence of God and the duty of witness.

name: A Tale of Two Cities
teaser: Dickens's 1859 novel of London and Paris during the French Revolution — resurrection, sacrifice, and the most famous ending in English fiction. The guillotine's shadow over a love story.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the wine cask breaks in the street and the shadows of the era are drawn, then the final pages. Notice how Dickens foreshadows the blood. Write what Carton's sacrifice claims about love and meaning.

name: David Copperfield
teaser: Dickens's 1850 autobiographical novel of David's rise from the blacking factory to the novelist's desk — with Mr. Micawber, Uriah Heep, and the warmth of the first-person. Dickens called it his favorite child.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the factory and the stepfather
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where David's childhood is shadowed by the Murdstones. Notice how Dickens draws on his own hidden past. Write how the first-person voice turns the novel into a search for a place to belong.

name: Hard Times
teaser: Dickens's 1854 novel of the industrial town Coketown and the school of 'facts' — the Gradgrind family raised on statistics, the circus girl Sissy Jupe, and the question of what humans actually need. Dickens's most political novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the schoolroom of facts
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gradgrind's school demands facts and only facts. Notice how Dickens opposes the circus to the countinghouse. Write what the novel says about education, imagination, and the steam engine's human cost.

name: The Pickwick Papers
teaser: Dickens's 1836 first novel — Mr. Pickwick and his club's comic rambles through England, with Sam Weller's proverbs and the Fleet prison's shadows. The book that made Dickens famous overnight.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the club and the first adventures
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Pickwick Club's expeditions begin in comedy. Notice how the serial structure keeps each chapter self-contained. Write how the novel's warmth — and its sudden turn to the debtors' prison — shows Dickens's range.

name: Nicholas Nickleby
teaser: Dickens's 1839 novel of Nicholas's fight against his uncle Ralph and the monstrous schoolmaster Wackford Squeers — a serial that attacked Yorkshire boarding schools and championed the underdog.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the family and the school
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Nickleby family's ruin sends Nicholas to Dotheboys Hall. Notice how Dickens builds the horror of Squeers through comedy. Write what the novel's crusade against child abuse achieved in its own time.

name: Tess of the d'Urbervilles
teaser: Hardy's 1891 novel of Tess Durbeyfield, 'a pure woman' destroyed by a society that will not let her be pure — the seduction, the murder, and the sacrifice at Stonehenge. Hardy's most beloved tragedy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the d'Urberville claim
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the family's false pedigree sets Tess's fate in motion. Notice how Hardy indicts the world rather than Tess. Write what the subtitle 'a pure woman' is arguing against, and how the ending completes the argument.

name: Far from the Madding Crowd
teaser: Hardy's 1874 novel of Bathsheba Everdene, the farm she inherits, and the three men who love her — the shepherd Gabriel Oak, the farmer Boldwood, and the soldier Troy. Hardy's sunniest great novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the meeting on the road
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gabriel Oak first sees Bathsheba and loses his flock. Notice how Hardy makes the Wessex landscape a character. Write what the title promises about the world the novel explores — and how the love plot tests it.

name: Jude the Obscure
teaser: Hardy's 1895 novel of Jude Fawley, the stonemason who dreams of Oxford — and of Sue Bridehead, with whom he breaks every rule. The novel that ended the Victorian novel, and Hardy's fiction career.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the dream of Christminster
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jude's longing for the university city is established. Notice how Hardy turns the institutions of class into the novel's villains. Write why the book so scandalized its readers — and what it demands we look at.

name: The Mayor of Casterbridge
teaser: Hardy's 1886 novel of Michael Henchard, who sells his wife at a fair and spends his life paying for it — a tragedy of character, corn markets, and the town that watches. 'Character is fate' made flesh.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the sale at the fair
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the drunken Henchard auctions his wife and wakes to the horror. Notice how Hardy presents the act and its lifelong consequences. Write how the novel's title — the man and the office — frames his rise and fall.

name: Silas Marner
teaser: George Eliot's 1861 novel of the weaver who hoards gold until it is stolen and a child arrives in its place — a fable about what money and love actually buy. Eliot's most perfect small book.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the weaver and the gold
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Silas's wronged past and his miserly present are established. Notice how Eliot makes the gold almost human. Write what the theft and the foundling Eppie teach Silas — and the novel's readers — about what is truly valuable.

name: The Mill on the Floss
teaser: Eliot's 1860 novel of Maggie Tulliver, too clever and too loving for her provincial world — and of the brother who cannot forgive her. The novel of family love and its ruin, ending in the flood.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mill and the children
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Maggie and Tom's childhood in the mill is established. Notice how Eliot grounds the tragedy in the economics of the family. Write what the river and the flood mean, and whether the ending is escape or punishment.

name: Adam Bede
teaser: Eliot's 1859 first novel — the carpenter Adam, the beautiful Hetty, and the infanticide at the heart of the English countryside. Eliot's warmest and most human story, rooted in her own childhood.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the workshop and the village
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the village world of Hayslope is established. Notice how Eliot's realism treats the poorest characters with full dignity. Write how the novel's sympathy — extended even to Hetty's crime — was radical for its time.

name: Romola
teaser: Eliot's 1863 historical novel set in Renaissance Florence — Romola, the scholar's daughter, and her brilliant faithless husband Tito, against the backdrop of Savonarola's city. Eliot's most ambitious book.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Florence and the marriage
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Romola's world of learning and Tito's charm are established. Notice how Eliot reconstructs Florence from its archives. Write what the novel says about the collision of ideals — Savonarola's, Tito's, Romola's — in a real city.

name: Shirley
teaser: Charlotte Brontë's 1849 novel of the West Riding, the Luddite riots, and two very different women — the quiet Caroline and the heiress Shirley, whose name she made a girl's name. Brontë's most social novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mill and the two women
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the mill owners and the workers' unrest are established. Notice how Brontë connects the industrial conflict to the women's restricted lives. Write what Shirley's independence meant in 1849, and why the novel names a new kind of heroine.

name: Villette
teaser: Charlotte Brontë's 1853 novel of Lucy Snowe, who goes alone to a Belgian city and teaches in a girls' school — the loneliest and most modern of Brontë's books, and the one she called her best.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the voyage and the school
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Lucy's solitary journey and her arrival at Madame Beck's school are narrated with cool control. Notice how Brontë withholds Lucy's feelings even as she shows them. Write what the novel's ambiguous ending leaves the reader to decide.

name: Agnes Grey
teaser: Anne Brontë's 1847 novel of a governess's trials in two impossible households — the quietest and most honest of the Brontë novels, and the sharpest portrait of the governess's life in English fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the first post
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Agnes's hopes for her first governess post meet the Bloomfield children's cruelty. Notice how Anne Brontë reports the indignities without melodrama. Write what the novel reveals about the status of the Victorian governess.

name: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall
teaser: Anne Brontë's 1848 novel of Helen Graham, who leaves her drunken husband and earns her own living — the first sustained feminist novel in English, shocking enough that her sister Charlotte suppressed a reprint.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the tenant arrives
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the village's gossip meets Helen's secrecy, then the diary that explains her flight. Notice how Brontë uses the frame to build suspense. Write what the novel risks by defending a wife's right to leave.

name: The Professor
teaser: Charlotte Brontë's 1857 novel, written before Jane Eyre and published after her death — William Crimsworth's years teaching in Brussels. Brontë's first attempt at the story she would perfect in Villette.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mill and the decision
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Crimsworth rejects his brother's mill and sails for the continent. Notice how Brontë's male narrator is cool where her female narrators are fierce. Write how this early novel prefigures Villette — and what changed in between.

name: North and South
teaser: Elizabeth Gaskell's 1855 novel of Margaret Hale, moved from the rural south to the industrial north — where the mill master John Thornton and the striking workers teach her a new England. The industrial novel's masterpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the move to Milton
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Margaret's displacement into the mill town is rendered with exactness. Notice how Gaskell gives both master and worker their arguments. Write what the novel proposes about the possibility of understanding across class lines.

name: The Bell Jar
teaser: Sylvia Plath's 1963 autobiographical novel of Esther Greenwood's summer in New York and her descent into breakdown — the fig tree, the bell jar, and the woman who must choose which self to be. The great novel of the gifted girl's suffocation.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the summer and the fig tree
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Esther's internship and her paralysis before the fig tree are established. Notice how Plath keeps the voice witty even at the edge. Write what the bell jar represents, and what lifting it requires.

name: Ariel
teaser: Plath's 1965 collection, assembled after her death — Lady Lazarus, Daddy, and the poems that made her a myth. A book of fury, transformation, and language pushed to its breaking point.

exploreAction.targetName: Lady Lazarus and Daddy
exploreAction.instruction: Read Lady Lazarus and Daddy aloud. Notice how Plath's rhymes and repetitions build unbearable pressure. Write what the poems do with anger — how does the speaker transform herself on the page, and what does the myth-making cost?

name: The Poetry of Robert Frost
teaser: Frost's New England poems — The Road Not Taken, Mending Wall, Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening — plain speech with terrible depths beneath. America's most beloved, and least simple, poet.

exploreAction.targetName: A selection of poems, including Stopping by Woods and Design
exploreAction.instruction: Read the famous poems, then a darker one like Design or Out, Out—. Notice how Frost's folksy voice turns suddenly strange. Write what the woods in the snow are really about, and why the speaker has 'miles to go before I sleep.'

name: Four Quartets
teaser: Eliot's 1943 sequence of four meditations — Burnt Norton, East Coker, The Dry Salvages, Little Gidding — on time, memory, and the still point of the turning world. The summit of Eliot's poetry.

exploreAction.targetName: Burnt Norton, the opening section
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Burnt Norton, where the rose garden and the passage of time are established. Notice how Eliot returns to the same images with different music. Write what 'the still point of the turning world' means, and how the poem circles toward it.

name: The Cantos
teaser: Ezra Pound's lifelong epic poem, published in fragments from 1917 to 1969 — a collage of history, economics, Chinese ideograms, and personal fury, 'a poem including history.' Monumental and maddening.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening cantos
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening cantos, where the descent into the underworld and the voyage are established. Notice how Pound cuts between voices, languages, and eras. Write how the poem's fragments enact its argument about civilization's decline.

name: Walden
teaser: Thoreau's 1854 account of two years in a cabin at Walden Pond — economy, solitude, and the deliberate life. The founding book of American nature writing and of every project of voluntary simplicity.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Economy and Where I Lived
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Thoreau itemizes his costs and his reasons. Notice how his ledger-keeping is a philosophy. Write what 'the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation' means, and whether the cabin experiment still speaks to you.

name: Civil Disobedience
teaser: Thoreau's 1849 essay born of a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax — on the duty of the individual against the state. The text that Gandhi and King carried into their movements.

exploreAction.targetName: The full essay
exploreAction.instruction: Read the essay, from the jail anecdote to the closing appeals. Notice how Thoreau's wit carries his radical claims. Write what he means by 'that government is best which governs least' — and how his standard of conscience applies to a citizen today.

name: Self-Reliance
teaser: Emerson's 1841 essay, the sermon of American individualism — 'trust thyself,' the nonconformist, and the wholeness of each soul. The text that every American rebel, from Whitman to the counterculture, was raised on.

exploreAction.targetName: The full essay
exploreAction.instruction: Read the essay, noticing how Emerson's aphorisms accumulate into a worldview. Write what he means by the 'aboriginal self' and by 'whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist.' Where do you agree — and where does the doctrine of self-trust need correction?

name: Nature
teaser: Emerson's 1836 manifesto that launched Transcendentalism — the transparent eyeball, the unity of the soul with nature, and the call to an original relation to the universe. American philosophy begins here.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Emerson describes the woods and the 'transparent eyeball.' Notice how he treats nature as both commodity and teacher. Write what the essay means by 'an original relation to the universe' — and whether we still need one.

name: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
teaser: Montaigne's 1580 invention of the essay — 'I am myself the matter of my book' — three volumes of digression, skepticism, and self-knowledge that taught Europe how to think in prose. The most companionable book ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: Of Cannibals and Of the Education of Children
exploreAction.instruction: Read two essays. Notice how Montaigne wanders from his title and returns by instinct. Write what 'que sais-je?' — what do I know? — asks of the reader, and why his self-portrait still feels like a mirror.

name: Meditations
teaser: Marcus Aurelius's private notebooks, written in Greek while emperor of Rome — the Stoic manual of self-discipline, mortality, and the duty of the moment. A ruler talking to himself, and to us.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One — the debts — and a later book
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book One, where Marcus lists what he owes his teachers and family, then a later book of maxims. Notice how the notebook form lets the philosophy breathe. Write which single precept you would carry into a difficult day, and why.

name: The Republic
teaser: Plato's dialogue on justice, the city, and the soul — the allegory of the cave, the philosopher king, and the question of why be just. The book that founded political philosophy.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One and the allegory of the cave in Book Seven
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book One, where the argument about justice begins, then the cave allegory. Notice how the dialogue keeps the reader arguing. Write what the cave's prisoners and the returning philosopher represent — and whether the philosopher should go back down.

name: Nicomachean Ethics
teaser: Aristotle's lectures on the good life — virtue as a mean, friendship as necessity, and happiness as activity of the soul. The most practical book of philosophy ever written, and the most humane.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One — happiness — and Book Two — virtue
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening books. Notice how Aristotle reasons from what we actually do. Write what his doctrine of the mean — courage between cowardice and recklessness — looks like applied to a real choice you face.

name: Confessions
teaser: Augustine's 400 AD spiritual autobiography — the pear theft, the tears, and 'late have I loved thee' — the first great memoir, and the model for every confession since, sacred or secular.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One and Book Eight — the conversion
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening books, where Augustine examines his infancy and his youth, then the garden scene of his conversion. Notice how the memoir turns memory into prayer. Write what the structure — confessing to God rather than to an audience — does to the story.

name: Summa Theologica
teaser: Thomas Aquinas's 13th-century summa of Christian philosophy — questions, objections, and replies arranged with architectural patience. The great synthesis of faith and reason, still argued with today.

exploreAction.targetName: A question on the existence of God
exploreAction.instruction: Read one question, like the five ways. Notice the method: objections first, then the reply, then replies to each objection. Write how the format itself models honest argument, and assess the strength of one of the 'ways.'

name: Leviathan
teaser: Hobbes's 1651 argument for the social contract — the state of nature as a war of all against all, and the sovereign needed to keep the peace. The book that made the modern state thinkable.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the state of nature
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Hobbes describes the state of nature and its 'nasty, brutish, and short' life. Notice how rigorously he derives authority from fear. Write what the theory assumes about human nature, and where his premises need testing.

name: Two Treatises of Government
teaser: Locke's 1689 argument for natural rights, property, and the consent of the governed — the philosophical foundation of the American and French revolutions, and of every liberal constitution since.

exploreAction.targetName: The second treatise, on civil government
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on the state of nature and property. Notice how Locke grounds government in consent rather than conquest. Write how his account of labor and property still shapes arguments about ownership and justice.

name: The Social Contract
teaser: Rousseau's 1762 tract that begins 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' — the general will, the legislator, and the theory of legitimate authority that both inspired and haunted revolutions.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Rousseau dissolves and rebuilds the foundations of society. Notice how compressed and prophetic his sentences are. Write what 'the general will' means, and why the concept has been used for both freedom and tyranny.

name: Common Sense
teaser: Thomas Paine's 1776 pamphlet that turned colonial grievance into the case for independence — written in a style 'calculated for the common reader.' The best-selling American book of its century.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Paine argues from 'simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense.' Notice how he speaks to the reader as an equal. Write what made the pamphlet so persuasive in 1776 — and whether its style still works.

name: Rights of Man
teaser: Paine's 1791 reply to Burke's attack on the French Revolution — a defense of natural rights, republicanism, and the poor, written with a fury that got him tried for treason in England.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Paine answers Burke's defense of inherited privilege. Notice how he treats government as an instrument of the people rather than a mystery. Write what 'the rights of man' meant then, and how far those rights now extend.

name: Fahrenheit 451
teaser: Ray Bradbury's 1953 novel of Montag the fireman who burns books — until the girl next door asks him if he is happy. The definitive American novel of censorship, and of the warmth that books give.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the fire and the meeting with Clarisse
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Montag's fire and wall-screens meet Clarisse's questions. Notice how Bradbury compresses the whole argument into image and scene. Write what the novel predicts about distraction, and what books are for.

name: Dandelion Wine
teaser: Bradbury's 1957 novel of a summer in Green Town, Illinois, in 1928 — Douglas Spaulding's twelve-year-old summer of time machines, magic sneakers, and the bottle that holds the season. The great novel of childhood's summer.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the summer begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Douglas's summer is declared and the magical sneakers appear. Notice how Bradbury's prose is drunk on the season. Write what the dandelion wine preserves — and what the novel says about the summer we carry all our lives.

name: Something Wicked This Way Comes
teaser: Bradbury's 1962 novel of two boys and a carnival that arrives at midnight in October — the carousel that reverses age, the mirror maze, and the dark showman. The greatest autumn novel ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the carnival arrives
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the lightning-rod salesman warns the boys and the carnival unloads. Notice how Bradbury makes autumn itself a character. Write what the carnival offers — and what it takes in payment.

name: The Body
teaser: Stephen King's 1982 novella of four boys who walk the railroad tracks to see a dead body — friendship, fear, and the summer that ends childhood. The basis of the film Stand by Me.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the walk begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gordie, Chris, Teddy, and Vern set out on the tracks. Notice how King renders boyhood talk with total fidelity. Write what the journey means to each boy — and what they find, besides the body.

name: The Shining
teaser: King's 1977 novel of the Overlook Hotel, its winter caretaker, and his son who shines — a family trapped with the hotel's history. The novel of addiction, rage, and the haunted places inside a family.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the interview and the closing
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jack Torrance's past and the hotel's offer are established. Notice how King uses the hotel's emptiness as pressure. Write what the novel says about the monsters a father carries — and what the hedge animals are doing.

name: It
teaser: King's 1986 thousand-page novel of Derry, Maine, and the shape-shifting horror that wakes every 27 years — seven children who fight it, and the adults they become. The great American novel of childhood fear and memory.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the storm and the paper boat
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Georgie's paper boat meets the clown. Notice how King moves between the children's 1958 and the adults' 1985. Write what It — the thing that wears your fear — says about the power of facing childhood terrors together.

name: Misery
teaser: King's 1987 novel of Paul Sheldon, the romance novelist held captive by his 'number one fan' Annie Wilkes — a single-room horror story about writing, obsession, and the reader who loves too much.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the crash and the captivity
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Paul wakes in Annie's house and begins to understand his situation. Notice how King builds horror from one room and two people. Write what the novel suggests about the relationship between writers and their most devoted readers.

name: The Dead Zone
teaser: King's 1979 novel of Johnny Smith, who wakes from a coma with the power to see the future by touch — and the glimpse of a politician that demands the hardest choice. The novel of the gift that is also a curse.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the accident and the awakening
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Johnny's accident and his slow awakening are established. Notice how King treats the power as a medical and moral condition. Write what the novel suggests about knowing the future — and the duty that comes with it.

name: Death on the Nile
teaser: Christie's 1937 novel of luxury river steamer, a honeymoon, and a murder — Poirot among the passengers where everyone has a motive and the jewels are not the only thing at stake. Sunlit, elegant, and perfectly engineered.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the cruise and the announcement
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the passengers board the Karnak and the love triangle is announced. Notice how Christie plants every clue in plain sight. Write how the setting — a boat on the Nile — both isolates the suspects and dazzles the reader.

name: The A.B.C. Murders
teaser: Christie's 1936 novel where the killer writes to Poirot to announce the next victim — a serial killer's alphabetical game that ends with one of the most audacious twists in detective fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the first letter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Poirot receives the letter and dismisses it. Notice how Christie uses the serial structure to expand the form. Write how the killer's vanity — writing to the detective — becomes the key to the solution.

name: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd
teaser: Christie's 1926 novel that outraged and delighted readers — the country-house murder narrated by the doctor, with an ending that changed the rules of detective fiction forever. The book every mystery must answer to.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the village and the murder
