teaser: Adolfo Bioy Casares's 1940 novel of a castaway on a deserted island who discovers a machine that replays the past — and falls in love with a ghost. Borges called it flawless.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journal and the visitors
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the castaway's journal decodes the island's impossible visitors. Notice how Bioy Casares keeps the mystery rigorously logical. Write how the novel uses science fiction to ask what it means to love someone who is an image.

name: The Grapes of Wrath
teaser: Steinbeck's 1939 Pulitzer-winning novel of the Joad family driven off the Oklahoma dust bowl toward California — the great American novel of the Depression, of the road, and of 'we.'

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the dust and the road
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the dust and the bank's eviction frame the Joads' journey. Notice how Steinbeck alternates the family chapters with the wider interchapters. Write what the interchapters — the turtle, the used-car lots — add to the family's story.

name: Of Mice and Men
teaser: Steinbeck's 1937 novella of George and Lennie, who carry their dream of a farm from ranch to ranch — a small perfect tragedy about friendship, strength, and the tenderness that destroys.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, from the clearing where the story opens and closes. Notice how Steinbeck builds the dream of the farm to make the ending land harder. Write what George's final act costs him, and what the novella says about mercy.

name: Cannery Row
teaser: Steinbeck's 1945 comic novel of the Monterey sardine street — Doc, Mack and the boys, and a party for a man who helps everyone. A celebration of the useless, generous, and broke.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the street and its characters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Steinbeck introduces the street as a character. Notice how he treats the community's plans and failures with affection. Write what Cannery Row proposes about success, purpose, and friendship.

name: My Ántonia
teaser: Willa Cather's 1918 novel of the Nebraska prairie and the immigrant girl Ántonia Shimerda — Jim Burden's memory of a childhood friendship that becomes the measure of his life. The great American pastoral.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journey to Nebraska
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jim and Ántonia arrive on the prairie as children. Notice how Cather renders the land as both harsh and holy. Write what Ántonia comes to mean to Jim — and why he calls her story his own.

name: Death Comes for the Archbishop
teaser: Willa Cather's 1927 novel of two French priests building a diocese across the desert Southwest — a saint's life, a travelogue, and a meditation on how place shapes a soul.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the bishop's journey
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Bishop Latour rides through a landscape older than his church. Notice how Cather slows time to the pace of the desert. Write how the novel's episodic structure mirrors the life it honors.

name: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
teaser: Thornton Wilder's 1927 Pulitzer-winning novella — when a Peruvian bridge collapses and five people fall, a friar investigates why God chose those five. A small perfect book about love and chance.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters and the final chapter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening, where the bridge falls and the investigation begins, then the closing meditation. Notice how Wilder weaves the five lives together. Write what the novel concludes about the 'why' the friar seeks — and whether an answer is possible.

name: Our Town
teaser: Thornton Wilder's 1938 play of Grover's Corners, New Hampshire — the milkman, the choir, the wedding, and the graveyard. A play that makes an ordinary life feel like the greatest mystery there is.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and Act Three
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where the Stage Manager introduces the town, then Act Three, where Emily returns to one ordinary day. Notice how the play's minimal staging forces attention onto the words. Write what 'Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?' asks of you.

name: Ethan Frome
teaser: Edith Wharton's 1911 novella of a Massachusetts farm, a sick wife, a young cousin, and one sled ride — a tragedy of the poor and silent, framed by the narrator who pieces together what happened.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, from the frame narrator's arrival in Starkfield to the sled ride's aftermath. Notice how Wharton builds the snow and the silence. Write what the smash-up costs each of the three, and why the story needs its frame.

name: The Age of Innocence
teaser: Edith Wharton's 1920 Pulitzer-winning novel of Newland Archer and the Countess Olenska in old New York — a society that punishes scandal while pretending to be innocent. The great novel of manners.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the opera and the engagement
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the opera box and the engagement announce the rules of Newland's world. Notice how Wharton narrates what cannot be said. Write what the novel says about the freedom that comes too late.

name: The Awakening
teaser: Kate Chopin's 1899 novel of Edna Pontellier, who wakes to her own desires in the summer heat of Grand Isle — and cannot fit back into the life that waits. The novel that scandalized and then defined an era.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the summer at Grand Isle
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Edna's awakening begins in the sea and the music. Notice how Chopin links the ocean with the self. Write what the final swim means — is it defeat, triumph, or something that is neither?

name: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets
teaser: Stephen Crane's 1893 novella of the Bowery — a girl, a brother, a neighborhood, and a fall written with the cold precision of a newspaper report. American naturalism's opening document.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, from the tenement childhood to the ending. Notice how Crane reports Maggie's tragedy without sentiment. Write what the novel's refusal to moralize achieves, and how its irony indicts the neighborhood that made it.

name: Sister Carrie
teaser: Theodore Dreiser's 1900 novel of Carrie Meeber, who arrives in Chicago with a trunk and rises — while the man who loves her falls. American naturalism's big-city epic of desire and drift.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the train to Chicago
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Carrie's arrival and her first disappointment are rendered with documentary exactness. Notice how Dreiser treats ambition as weather. Write what the novel suggests about luck, want, and the machinery of the city.

name: The Jungle
teaser: Upton Sinclair's 1906 novel of the Lithuanian immigrant Jurgis Rudkus in Chicago's meatpacking yards — the novel that made America change its food laws. Socialism, slaughter, and a family eaten alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wedding and the yards
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the wedding feast and the packinghouse set Jurgis's hopes and their end. Notice how Sinclair piles fact on fact to indict the system. Write how the novel's reformist argument works through one family's ruin.

name: Progress and Poverty
teaser: Henry George's 1879 treatise asking why poverty grows alongside progress — and proposing the single tax on land. A book that moved millions and shaped labor, land, and urban policy worldwide.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the riddle of poverty amid progress
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where George states the paradox the book will answer. Notice how he argues in plain, forceful prose. Write what his diagnosis — that land speculation captures the gains of growth — suggests about cities today.

name: Up from Slavery
teaser: Booker T. Washington's 1901 autobiography — from a Virginia slave cabin to founding Tuskegee Institute — a self-help epic and one of the most influential and contested books in Black American history.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — slavery and freedom
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Washington describes emancipation and his hunger for education. Notice how he frames progress as gradual and practical. Write how his philosophy of accommodation was both praised and fiercely criticized by his contemporaries.

name: The Souls of Black Folk
teaser: W. E. B. Du Bois's 1903 collection of essays that gave the world 'double consciousness' and the color line — part sociology, part memoir, part hymn. The founding text of modern Black thought.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — of our spiritual strivings
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapter, where Du Bois describes the veil and double consciousness. Notice how he blends history, statistics, and personal testimony. Write what 'two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings' means, and whether the problem he names has changed.

name: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
teaser: Douglass's 1845 memoir of his enslavement and escape — the whip, the learning to read, the fight with Covey — written to prove he was a man, and the most powerful American testimony of its century.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — learning to read
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Douglass is taught letters and then forbidden them. Notice how he narrates the growth of his own mind under slavery. Write what the book says about literacy as freedom, and how the fight with Covey turns him into a man.

name: Uncle Tom's Cabin
teaser: Harriet Beecher Stowe's 1852 novel that Lincoln reportedly greeted as the cause of the Civil War — the sentimental epic of Tom, Eliza, and the fugitives. The most consequential novel in American history.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the sale and Eliza's flight
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Tom is sold down the river and Eliza crosses the ice with her child. Notice how Stowe uses the reader's sympathy as a political weapon. Write how the novel's sentimentality both moved history and has since been complicated.

name: Little House on the Prairie
teaser: Laura Ingalls Wilder's 1935 novel of the Ingalls family's covered-wagon year on the Kansas prairie — the second book of the series that made pioneer childhood a national memory.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journey west
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the family crosses rivers and builds a house of logs. Notice how Wilder renders the prairie through a child's senses. Write what the book preserves — and what it quietly leaves out — about westward expansion.

name: Tarzan of the Apes
teaser: Edgar Rice Burroughs's 1912 novel of the English lord raised by apes in the African jungle — the adventure that became a century of movies, comics, and arguments. Read as pure myth, it still moves.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the cabin and the apes
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the infant Tarzan is orphaned and adopted. Notice how Burroughs narrates the boy's education in the jungle with relish. Write how the novel's premise — nature versus nurture — made it so durable, and so contested.

name: The Dark Forest
teaser: Liu Cixin's 2008 second volume of the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy — humanity prepares for an alien invasion centuries away, and a man must decide whether the universe is a forest of hunters.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wallfacers
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the wallfacers are chosen to deceive the enemy by deceiving everyone. Notice how Liu Cixin thinks at the scale of centuries. Write what the 'dark forest' theory claims about contact between civilizations.

name: Ball Lightning
teaser: Liu Cixin's 2004 novel of a scientist obsessed with the mystery his parents were killed by — ball lightning — and the weapon it can become. Hard SF about the strange marriage of weather and war.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the storm and the obsession
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Chen's parents vanish in a lightning strike and his life's question is set. Notice how Liu Cixin grounds cosmic speculation in precise physics. Write how the novel uses an unexplained phenomenon to explore obsession and sacrifice.

name: Solaris
teaser: Stanisław Lem's 1961 novel of a scientist sent to a station above the ocean planet Solaris — where the ocean's contact takes the shape of your deepest guilt. The great novel of unknowable otherness.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Kelvin's arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Kelvin arrives at the station and the strange visitors are already there. Notice how Lem refuses to explain the ocean away. Write what the novel suggests about the limits of understanding — and whether contact is possible at all.

name: The Dispossessed
teaser: Le Guin's 1974 novel of Shevek, a physicist from the anarchist moon Anarres who travels to the capitalist planet Urras — 'an ambiguous utopia' that questions both worlds. The novel that made 'anarchist' a literary ideal.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Anarres and the wall
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Shevek's departure from Anarres is narrated against memories of his utopia. Notice how Le Guin structures the novel in alternating worlds. Write what the novel says about freedom, solidarity, and the walls we build.

name: The Martian Chronicles
teaser: Bradbury's 1950 linked story cycle of the colonization of Mars — a bittersweet mirror held up to Earth, where the Martians die of chicken pox and the humans bring their own doom. The prose is pure poetry.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening stories — the rockets and the Martians
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening stories, from the rockets to the Martians' last telepathic moments. Notice how Bradbury treats Mars as a state of mind. Write how the collection uses the frontier to comment on Earth's own history.

name: Rendezvous with Rama
teaser: Clarke's 1973 novel of an alien cylinder entering the solar system — a first-contact story with no contact, a mystery with no answer. Hard SF's most elegant demonstration of wonder without explanation.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the detection of Rama
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where humanity watches Rama's approach with growing awe. Notice how Clarke makes the reader feel the scale of the artifact. Write what the novel gains by never explaining who built Rama or why.

name: Brave New World Revisited
teaser: Huxley's 1958 nonfiction sequel — written thirty years after his novel, he examines the actual techniques of control: propaganda, drugs, and the 'managed democracy' he feared more than Orwell's totalitarian state.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the prophecy and its tools
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Huxley compares his own predictions with the world of 1958. Notice how he updates his fictional warnings with real politics and psychology. Write which of his control techniques you see most clearly in your own media diet.

name: Going Postal
teaser: Terry Pratchett's 2004 Discworld novel of Moist von Lipwig, a con man given a choice — run the post office or die — who discovers that running a failing institution is the greatest con of all.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the hanging and the offer
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Moist's 'execution' becomes a job offer. Notice how Pratchett builds comedy out of institutional absurdity. Write what the novel says about bureaucracy, communication, and the art of making things work.

name: Small Gods
teaser: Pratchett's 1992 Discworld novel of Brutha, the only believer left in the god Om — who has been reduced to a tortoise. A novel about faith, institutions, and what happens when belief becomes bureaucracy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the tortoise and the novice
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Om the tortoise and Brutha the simple novice meet. Notice how Pratchett uses the size of the god as a joke with theology inside it. Write what the novel says about the difference between religion and belief.

name: Norse Mythology
teaser: Neil Gaiman's 2017 retelling of the Norse myths — Odin, Thor, and Loki from the creation to Ragnarök, told in a storyteller's voice that makes the old gods feel like old friends.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the creation and the mead
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, from the void Ginnungagap to the building of Asgard. Notice how Gaiman keeps the myths episodic and wry. Write what the Norse gods' flaws — Loki's tricks, Thor's temper — reveal about what these myths were for.

name: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
teaser: Gaiman's 2013 novella of a man who returns to his childhood home and remembers the girl at the end of the lane, the monsters, and the ocean that was really there. Memory as the deepest fantasy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the return and the lane
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the narrator's return unlocks the past. Notice how Gaiman keeps the adult and child narrators in the same breath. Write what the ocean at the end of the lane is, and what the book says about childhood's magic.

name: The Graveyard Book
teaser: Gaiman's 2008 Newbery-winning novel of Nobody Owens, raised by the dead in a graveyard after his family is murdered — a coming-of-age story where the ghosts are the best parents. The Jungle Book with tombstones.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Nobody and the man Jack
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the toddler escapes the murderer and is adopted by the graveyard. Notice how Gaiman makes the dead warm and the living threatening. Write how the book uses the graveyard's lessons — history, silence, mortality — to raise a child.

name: Hogfather
teaser: Pratchett's 1996 Discworld novel — with the Hogfather missing, Death must take his place and deliver the toys, while Susan tries to save the sun from being switched off. A novel about belief, from the most beloved of fantasy satirists.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the assassins and the list
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the plot to kill the Hogfather is set in motion. Notice how Pratchett wraps serious questions about belief in slapstick. Write what the book's famous lines — about how humans need fantasy to stay human — mean to you.

name: Assassin's Apprentice
teaser: Robin Hobb's 1995 first novel of the Realm of the Elderlings — Fitz, a royal bastard trained as an assassin and bonded to a wolf, in a kingdom of scheming courtiers. The fantasy of quiet, painful intimacy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the boy left at the keep
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the six-year-old Fitz is abandoned at Buckkeep. Notice how Hobb narrates from inside Fitz's wounded, watchful perspective. Write how the novel builds its magic — the Skill and the Wit — around loneliness and loyalty.

name: Gideon the Ninth
teaser: Tamsyn Muir's 2019 novel of necromancers, a locked-tomb trial, and Gideon Nav — a swordswoman who would rather be anywhere else. Lesbian necromancers in space, with a voice like a meme and a heart like a gothic novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Ninth House and the invitation
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gideon's escape plans keep failing and the Emperor's summons arrives. Notice how Muir balances snark and gothic grandeur. Write how the novel's outrageous premise becomes genuinely moving by the end.

name: All Systems Red
teaser: Martha Wells's 2017 first Murderbot novella — a self-hacking security android that would rather watch media than protect its clients, until it decides to anyway. The most beloved robot in modern science fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the survey team and the murderbot
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Murderbot's deadpan narration introduces its media habit and its job. Notice how Wells makes the reader care about a character who insists it doesn't care. Write what Murderbot's name — and its refusal to be called a 'SecUnit' — reveals.
